In evaluating the potential of cancer therapies to be effective, it's essential to analyze the level of tumor cell infiltration and the strength of the immune system's reaction. To achieve this, AI models can be applied to histopathological images of tumor samples, which require high-quality training datasets. However, compiling and utilizing such datasets poses significant challenges due to the need for incorporating multiple training datasets and protecting sensitive clinical information. This problem can be resolved by a novel approach called FedCAT, an adaptive federated learning algorithm designed to train AI models for classifying immune cells in tumors by pooling data from multiple participants across a network. FedCAT overcomes existing federated learning limitations by allowing models to adapt to varying data quality and size across participants. In experiments, FedCAT successfully trained a deep learning model to accurately identify three types of tumor cell infiltration by leveraging five datasets compiled from 1,843 high-resolution images. Compared to other approaches, FedCAT achieved superior performance on an independent test set consisting of 1,512 images. The model's effectiveness was further validated against three commercial AI diagnostic tools. In addition, FedCAT was applied to analyze 13,000 high-resolution images from six datasets, classifying lymphocytic tumor cell infiltrations in 77% of cases. The code for FedCAT has been made available on GitHub. By resolving the technical challenge of training AI models for tumor cell infiltration classification, this work paves the way for further development of this application across multiple fields. In particular, this solution can be adapted to enhance the performance of models in other classification tasks, such as grading tumors, identifying cardiovascular disease, and analyzing colon polyps. In experiments involving the evaluation of FedCAT's performance, the model's accuracy was found to increase from 64% to 77% on the University of Michigan colon polyp dataset, and from 71% to 85% on the Idrija dataset used to analyze cardiovascular disease. In addition, FedCAT successfully trained a model that accurately identified three types of tumors 85% of the time. This work also explored the application of FedCAT to the development of shared models for segmenting tumors from normal tissue, a task on which the model performed well but was prone to overestimating the area of tumor cell infiltration. To address this challenge, a solution involving the use of a novel loss function was proposed but found to have a limited impact. Further research is needed to fully address the technical challenges surrounding the development of shared models for accurately identifying areas of tumor cell infiltration. This paper addresses the significant distortion caused by the underwater environment in fiber-optic communications, specifically the nonlinear chromatic dispersion that hinders high-speed data transfer.  To counter this effect, a decision-feedback equalizer was developed and successfully tested at high speeds over long distances in real-world underwater applications.  However, implementation of this equalizer was hindered by the high frequency errors that occurred, particularly in the FDDI interface.  To overcome this limitation, we incorporated an error-correction code known as Burst-Error Corrector, which significantly improved the performance of the equalizer.  The combination of this equalizer and error-correction code allowed for error-free transmission at 622 Mbps over 25 km and 45 Mbps over 100 km in real-world underwater settings.  We also investigated different code modulation schemes, demonstrating that the proposed technique can correct for up to 10% frequency errors with no deterioration in performance.  This breakthrough enables the safe and efficient transmission of data over long underwater distances using fiber-optic communications.  A practical application of this innovation is presented, where we successfully recovered over 99% of the data from a submerged underwater video tape, offering a promising prospect for the revival of underwater video archives.  Furthermore, we explored ways to integrate this technology with multiple fiber-optic cables, which has the potential to substantially increase data transfer speeds over underwater paths.  While some challenges still need to be addressed, this breakthrough paves the way for a range of innovative underwater communication systems and the revival of submerged data archives. This decrease in efficiency is attributed to the slow computation of memory-based convolutional layers. To rectify this issue, this paper introduces a novel kernel reduction method called Trim In Time (PIT) that minimizes memory usage and accelerates TCN training. In experiments, PIT demonstrated superior performance compared to alternative memory trimming approaches. Furthermore, our method is highly effective at compressing TCNs for computer vision tasks, achieving notable reductions in memory consumption and latency. Comprehensive evaluation of PIT was conducted across four benchmark datasets for video analysis, resulting in impressive accuracy gains following optimization. Notably, a TCN modeled after a 2D Convolutional Recurrent Network achieved exceptional performance on Lane Detection, outperforming the baseline by 8.5% in F-score. The optimized TCN also exhibited a latency reduction of over 5 times for Lane Detection and Action Recognition on the ActivityNet dataset. To facilitate widespread adoption of real-time TCNs, our method provides a solution for further optimizing these networks in conjunction with our trim-in-time code being openly accessible at https://github.com/GoogleResearch/trim-in-time. The code has since been incorporated into the popular open-source deep learning framework, TensorFlow Transform. The transformation code can be found at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/tree/main/tensorflow-transform/examples/trim_in_time. Additionally, a pre-trained, highly optimized TCN for Lane Detection and Action Recognition on the ActivityNet dataset is accessible at https://github.com/GoogleResearch/trim-in-time. This pre-trained model serves as a prime example of the exceptional performance achievable with our trimming-in-time method. In particular, the optimized TCN model for Action Recognition weighs approximately 12MB, in comparison to the unoptimized 177MB. The notable memory reduction achieved with our method makes it highly suitable for applications involving real-time, memory-constrained devices. A search for additional rotation periods was conducted but no further ones were found down to a minimum detection threshold of 10 times the estimated primary period.  A comparison with other bulge clusters that have had their rotation periods assessed showed that Tonantzintla 2 rotates the slowest.  A theoretical model used to simulate the cluster's light curve based on its rotation period and the presence of blue horizontal branch stars failed to fully match the observed data from the CAPOS survey. The Yang-Lee edge singularity serves as a critical point for a second-order phase transition in systems that can be defined by a symmetry-based O(N) universality class, such as the O(N) $\sigma$-model. To understand the functional role of this edge in the universality class, we examine the critical surface of the Yang-Lee edge in the O(N) universality space by determining the minimum number of universality parameters required to position the edge's critical point. Our analysis indicates that this edge exhibits a complex, irreducible structure under the constraints of universal behavior and is defined by a distinct set of variables that are independent of the symmetry-based O(N) parameters. Consequently, we establish that the Yang-Lee edge's critical point is placed at the intersection of three independent paths that correspond to critical behaviors in the O(N) universality class along the following routes: the Ising barrier in the O(1+1) Percolation path, the tricritical line in the O(2) universality class, and the critical endpoint in the O(2+1) Percolation path. Additionally, we establish a direct relationship between the Yang-Lee edge's surface and the deconfinement transition's surface in Z(N) universality classes. Our analysis also reveals that the edge's critical point exhibits a first-order character for N equal to one and an infinite-order phase transition for N equal to two. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical surface of the Yang-Lee edge over N values intersects the self-dual line at a critical point that holds N-2 independent variables and exhibits an infinite-order phase transition for any N value greater than or equal to two. Our research provides a clear, detailed understanding of the Yang-Lee edge's critical point and its relationship to universal behavior across all O(N) universality classes. It enables us to analyze the functional role of this edge in the universality class and to establish a direct connection between the Yang-Lee edge's critical point and critical points found in other transitions, such as the deconfinement transition in Z(N) universality classes. Our findings also highlight the complex, irreducible structure of the Yang-Lee edge's critical surface and its relationship to constraints of universal behavior. It is essential to note that all predictions derived from our analysis can be verified through numerical simulations. In this research, we enhance the performance of pose estimation by incorporating two key techniques: Correspondence Field Learning and Shape Normalization Using Clustering in 2D projections of 3D data. The proposed framework, named DeepHMap++, utilizes multiple clumping strategies to efficiently reduce dimensional data while preserving crucial information. This method employs Clustering in 3D space to normalize shape data, followed by the projection of encoded data onto 2D using shape-preserving techniques. As a result, DeepHMap++ exhibits enhanced performance in estimating a object's pose in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by improved results on the LINEMOD and IOWAS datasets. An in-depth examination of PD's numerical implementation and recent extensions to fluid-like behavior is also provided. Finally, the review concludes with an overview of ongoing challenges and potential paths for further research in this field. Geosteering during well placement presents opportunities for oil companies to lower costs and increase chances of hitting targeted reservoirs. Operators make critical decisions based on logging-while-drilling data combined with static models, yet these decisions can be compromised by inaccuracies in the data, models, and formation properties. To address this issue, we propose an original method that utilizes uncertainty quantification to analyze well logs and update the probabilities of formation properties, ultimately informing decisions in real-time. By combining the Hartigan diplog algorithm with sampling techniques, we analyze well logs to identify clusters of similar properties, estimate formation densities, and determine parameter uncertainties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with data from the North Sea. Results show that it effectively identifies density clusters, estimates formation densities accurately, and provides a clear framework for assessing parameter uncertainties that can guide operators' decisions. Ultimately, our approach represents a significant advancement in the field, and we believe it can be applied to various drilling scenarios. Additionally, we explore the integration of our method with geosteering services and highlight several improvements, including enhanced display options and operational recommendations. We also demonstrate the application of our method to more complex well logs and discuss potential extensions to multiple well logs, statistical modeling, and real-time visualization. By implementing this method in the field, we can provide a level of scientific rigor to drilling decisions and improve the effectiveness of geosteering services. Furthermore, we highlight several opportunities for further development and highlight a project that could test the method's performance in a field trial. Ultimately, our approach provides a scientific framework for real-time decision making and can be integrated with industry experts' knowledge and experience. Additionally, we emphasize the need for collaboration between service companies, operators, and academia to advance the field through shared data and knowledge. Lastly, we stress that the name "dip-structure" is a more accurate representation of our method's goals and we propose it for consideration. Finally, we believe that our method could be applied to various drilling scenarios and we stress the importance of collaboration and data sharing in the industry. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on identifying entities within other entities. Most existing studies tackle this challenge as a mere hierarchical task, applying conventional sequential models and merging them with techniques for handling hierarchy. In contrast, our work views nested NER as an integrated approach to analyze a text's overall structure. We introduce the NNEDA model, which combines hierarchical and non-hierarchical representations of text structure. NNEDA employs a holistic entity structure, incorporating all potential entities at various nesting levels, to guide its identification of nested entities. This model achieves superior performance on the standard WNUT2017 dataset, outperforming the best previous nested model by a significant 14.8% in F1-score. Furthermore, NNEDA exhibits adaptability and efficiency in handling real-world applications, as evidenced by its excellent performance on a specially created evaluation dataset comprising practical scenarios. Our approach opens up new research directions for nested NER, including the exploration of entity structures in other NLP tasks and the development of more sophisticated models to accommodate complex entity hierarchies. In particular, we explore the application of entity structures in coreference resolution and propose the use of hierarchical models for resolving inter-level conflicts. Overall, our work demonstrates the value of integrating text structure analysis for achieving superior performance in nested NER. Transitioning from sequential models to holistic structure analysis has also inspired new research directions in other NLP tasks. For instance, we discovered that the concept of holistic structure analysis can be pertinent to solving the limit issue in few-shot learning through the creation of a holistic learning framework. This framework titled Multi-Structure Few-Shot Learning has been successfully tested on the Mini-IMRE dataset. The results show that learning from a combination of simple and complex structures enables the model to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the target task. This technique has further implications for other areas in which the limit issue poses a significant challenge, and we believe that our approach has the potential to tackle such problems more effectively. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that makes use of the unique characteristics of different wireless communication technologies to enhance localization precision. In line with recent research, we assume that each target location can be represented by a unique point within a spherical area centered on the average location of beacons that have previously been accurately positioned. While code-mixing, the practice of switching between languages within a single utterance, message, or text may seem challenging at first, it is a common and accepted form of expression in multilingual communities. Nonetheless, current Natural Language Processing Systems exhibit significant difficulties in handling code-mixed data, limiting their potential to support vital functions such as language learning, user engagement, and cultural exchange. Ultimately, the paper calls for greater recognition of code-ming language as a normal language phenomenon and stresses the need for more research to unlock its full potential with Multilingual NLP. Human-based evaluation is the current standard for measuring visual image description quality, which relies on expensive and time-consuming methods. We propose two innovative approaches to overcome these limitations. First, we create a new, cost-effective method for compiling a set of high-quality reference datasets to train machine learning models. Second, we utilize advanced neural network techniques to enhance the accuracy of automatic image captioning. Specifically, we use multi-task learning, where we train a system to generate not only captions but also other descriptive outputs like visual features and image embeddings. We apply this approach to evaluate our proposed method with human subjects. Unsurprisingly, results show that using reference datasets compiled by humans as the gold standard yields better scores compared to our proposed method. However, surprisingly, when we introduce slight variations to the dataset, we find that human judgments are less precise than expected in distinguishing significant differences. We explore various factors that influence the accuracy of human judgments, including how they interpret system output as either correct or incorrect. We also observe that humans exhibit distinct preferences when it comes to selecting more descriptive output, such as caption lengths, from alternative formats like visual features. Our key findings contribute valuable insights to the field of machine learning, particularly in computer vision, where system evaluation is often complicated by the absence of reliable objective metrics. High-dimensional output from neural network models and the subjectivity inherent in human judgments only add to these challenges. As a result, we believe that our proposed method offers a viable solution to the ongoing debate about the superiority of neural network-based models. We have made our reference datasets and implementation publicly available for the benefit of the research community. When comparing our proposed method to alternative evaluation approaches, we conducted comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate the accuracy of our method, as validated by both human subjects and automated evaluation protocols. We have achieved notable improvements over previous state-of-the-art models on several metrics, including significant gains on challenging cases. Our innovative technique of compiling high-quality reference datasets in conjunction with advanced machine learning architectures has enabled us to achieve these results. We have introduced a new protocol for compiling reference datasets that offers a superior alternative to traditional human-based evaluation methods. This approach not only reduces the costs associated with compiling such datasets but also yields reliable gold standard data. We have applied our proposed method to evaluate the performance of machine learning models on two diverse benchmark datasets. Despite being simple, our calculated results using first-principles simulations reveal that the Ta-O framework is intricate, consisting of multiple interconnecting layers that make achieving a perfect, bulk-like crystal state difficult. To account for the effects of point defects that inevitably arise during growth, we developed a Monte Carlo algorithm to incorporate the influence of oxygen vacancies in the calculations. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the difficulty in achieving perfect, bulk-like crystal properties of Ta2O5 may be attributed to a combination of its structural properties and the high concentration of point defects that form during growth. Previous studies have analyzed the connection between the online network of communities and the dissemination of misinformation but have often overlooked the underlying geographic structure of this network. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed to integrate geographic data into network analysis. Utilizing Reddit data and a geographic mapping method, researchers identified distinct regional patterns across the US and a densely interconnected area they labeled the "Big Geographic Arrangement" (BGA). By applying network analysis and cultural transmission theories to BGA, it was discovered that information spread faster within BGA than outside of it. Furthermore, a designed simulation revealed that online misinformation transmission is influenced by cultural homophily. Additionally, a constructed model, informed by the underlying structure of the online network and the BGA, demonstrated accuracy in predicting the spread of misinformation. Teaching robots via demonstration relies on the interpretation of various auditory feedback by learning from instructed actions. Despite the significance of sound data in enhancing this process, little research has focused on analyzing the essential characteristics of instructive sounds, particularly within unstructured environments. This paper addresses this underexplored area by analyzing the acoustic features of human instructors' feedback when teaching a robot about object manipulation tasks. Our findings reveal that instructive sounds exhibit distinct patterns in various aspects, including duration, frequency content, and spectral characteristics. Specifically, we observed that humans utilize a diverse range of auditory indicators, encompassing sound emissions produced intentionally or unintentionally, with certain sounds being closely correlated with gravity's impact and others tied to the robot's performance. Our analysis also reveals that sound patterns vary significantly across different grasping techniques, suggesting that little standardization exists across human instructors' feedback. Intuitively, this implies that learning from auditory data in a manner independent of the source could be challenging. To further investigate this concept, we developed a series of experiments designed to compare the performance of models trained on data from a single human instructor with those trained on combined data from multiple human instructors. Our results indicate that models trained on data from a single source exhibit improved accuracy when evaluating the robot's manipulated objects through auditory feedback. This finding suggests that developing robot instructors who can optimize their feedback for the human teacher's preferences may be an effective strategy to enhance the accuracy of their demonstrations. Our analysis provides a comprehensive auditory analysis of human-instructed robot learning from demonstration, laying a solid foundation for exploring ways to enhance the process by designing optimal auditory feedback. This research is particularly relevant to areas like cross-domain learning and developing more flexible teaching methods that accommodate varied human instructors' feedback. Our study is a critical step in comprehending the complex patterns of human-instructed sound data, providing valuable insights that can be applied to various learning from demonstration tasks. This note provides an overview of various complex phenomena in geometric fluid dynamics, explaining how these difficulties arise from the unsolved Euler-Arnold equations. Specifically, it discusses how these challenges are interconnected and rooted in the broad framework of geometric fluid dynamics. Some key concepts, including the Carnot group, transport equations, and Lie-derivative-driven balance equations, are introduced to facilitate this exploration of the underlying principles and methods used to analyze the Euler-Arnold equations. A notable application is the examination of a geometric model for active fluids that maintains its connection to the Euler-Arnold equations and is shown to yield an explicit solution. This solution reveals a fascinating phenomenon in which the fluid's microstructure induces a persistent geometric effect that is linked to a non-trivial intersection of curves and surfaces. This intricate detail may have implications for the microscopic interpretation of higher-order Euler-Arnold equations. A supplementary chapter is also included, addressing a higher-order equation related to the geodesic equation on a Lie group, and some additional remarks on its solutions are provided. This work is a follow-up to the author's previous paper published in Journal of Non-Newtonian Fluid Mechanics. That paper focused on the fundamental properties of the Euler-Arnold equations, while this note delves into more intricate aspects of geometric fluid dynamics. According to predictions made by the Tyche model, the gravitational effect of an unseen planet should have a notable impact on the orbits of the known planets. Specifically, it should cause a measurable shift in the perihelion point of the Earth over time. However, after calculating this phenomenon for various Earth-Sun-Planet X configurations, we found that the effect is in fact very small and falls within the range of uncertainties in astronomical measurements. Consequently, we cannot expect to detect the presence of an unseen planet like Tyche through the observation of the perihelion shift of the Earth over a limited period of time. This does not discount the possibility of confirming Tyche's existence by analyzing older astronomical data. For the Earth's perihelion, we determined that the shift would be approximately 0.03 degrees over a 100-year period, which is an exceptionally small quantity. In contrast, we found that the perihelion of Neptune is more sensitive to the gravitational influence of an unseen planet like Tyche, and therefore analyzing its motion could provide valuable insights into this problem. A deeper examination of the Tyche model's predictions is necessary to fully comprehend the observational limitations imposed by the theory's parameters. Nevertheless, we are confident that our initial analysis has a solid foundation. In our research, we based our calculations on a key assumption concerning the Earth's orbit. As a result, we recommend that any analysis of this problem should take into account both the orbital period and the ecliptic motion of the affected planet. This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which established the short-term existence and uniqueness of the Yamabe flow on bounded domains with initially sign-changing potentials. This research extends those findings by demonstrating that the Yamabe flow converges to a steady state for certain initial data under minimal topological conditions. Specifically, it shows that if the boundary of the domain has a topological dimension of less than or equal to 0, or if the domain is the unit sphere in Euclidean space, then the Yamabe flow converges to a steady state with zero trace. This achievement is a significant consequence of the new proof of the conformal Harnack type inequality for fractional curvature equations. This proof, in turn, relies on a systematic approach involving a monotonicity formula and a stability estimate. This research also provides a foundation for further exploration into the long-term dynamics of the Yamabe flow on bounded domains. In an appendix, the technique of proving the conformal Harnack type inequality is applied to a broader class of fractional curvature equations under conformal transformations. This extension has implications for the stability of the Yamabe steady state. In particular, it shows that if the Yamabe steady state has zero trace and the same conformal volume as the sphere in Euclidean space, then it is smooth. This result holds for domains with boundaries of low topological dimension or unit spheres in Euclidean space. In such cases, if the Yamabe flow shares these geometric features with the sphere in Euclidean space, then it converges to the Yamabe steady state with zero trace. In an independent development, this result is shown to be true for all domains with boundaries of low topological dimension or unit spheres in Euclidean space, provided that the conformal volume of the sphere in Euclidean space is an isosceles angle of $\pi/4$. This extension holds for the fractional Yamabe flow on bounded domains and yields a new proof of the Chen-Nash inequality. In an even more independent development, this research is shown to be a consequence of the work of the second author with Daskalatos and Vazquez. In the context of categorization, a key concept is that of prototypes - a prototypical instance representing an entire class. This idea has been incorporated into the Prototypical Neural Network model, which uses prototypes to train a neural network on new data. However, traditional approaches require an ample amount of data from each class to define the prototypes, which can be problematic when working with small data sets. This paper proposes an innovative method to determine prototypes without relying on extensive data from each class. In our approach, we first establish a score for the quality of each data point based on how closely it aligns with other members of its own class and those of other classes. We then employ this quality score in an inverse-proportional manner to refine the prototypes through a process of re-weighting and re-normalizing. Our method achieves notable improvements over baseline models, even when working with extremely small data sets. A further analysis of our results is presented in the accompanying paper. This score-based approach enables us to successfully integrate our method with techniques for learning from multiple experts. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/protlearn. Cross-domain collaborative filtering is a highly sought-after technique to boost
recommendation systems' accuracy by leveraging information across multiple
databases. In many real-world scenarios, the primary challenge lies not in
identifying connections between domains but rather in exploiting relevant
information within a single domain due to its inherent complexity. To tackle
this issue, existing domain-specific techniques often employ different methods,
such as popularity-based and hybrid approaches, but they usually overlook the
diversity within a domain or focus on exclusive item selection. Furthermore,
most existing cross-domain and domain-specific techniques assume a linear
underlying structure, although it has been proven that latent factors can capture
the complexity of user preferences more effectively. To address these limitations,
we introduce an improved two-stage framework called Cooperative Recommendation
via Enhanced Aspect Learning. Initially, a new filter method determines a more
comprehensive set of items to rate by considering their popularity and
hierarchy. Subsequently, an efficient learner uses a new optimization technique
and a non-linear underlying structure to model users' diverse preferences more
accurately. Our experimental results on three large-scale datasets demonstrate
that our proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-
art approaches. To further validate our method's effectiveness, we conduct an
exensive statistical analysis to rule out random successes. Our framework's
efficacy is also proven to be cost-effective in terms of computational resources.

Our research aims to overcome this limitation by introducing an open-source Julia package called Hypatia, designed to accurately represent organic conic formulations as their own subproblems, thereby enabling the application of nested algorithms. The increasing complexity of medical imaging procedures such as MRI scans presents a challenge for effective image quality assessment. Currently utilized methods based on technical parameters like signal intensity, spatial resolution, and scan time fall short as they only consider a narrow range of factors and fail to account for the unique interactions between MRI settings that result in optimal image quality. Furthermore, traditional approaches relying solely on expert opinions are not scalable and do not facilitate the development of scalable and generalized protocols for optimizing MRI procedures. In response to these limitations, we propose a data-driven method for predicting optimal MRI configurations from existing datasets with varied characteristics. By combining multiple dimensions of data attributes including image features, technical parameters, and diagnostic information our approach achieves notable improvements in its scalability and generalization capabilities. However, evaluating the performance of such a predictive model in new situations remains a challenge as there may be a disparity between the data used to train it and the data it is being applied to. In the context of our MRI quality assessment task, this issue becomes particularly acute as there is a disparity between the training and validation datasets in terms of the variety of diagnostic protocols included. In order to address this concern and ensure the reliability of our model we have implemented a rigorous testing protocol that involves conducting a thorough evaluation of its performance on tightly controlled diagnostic datasets with limited protocol diversity. The foundation theorem is a significant concept in combinatorics, particularly relevant to the object class of involutions within the symmetric group $S_n$. This paper extends the foundation theorem to the finite classical Coxeter group $B_n$, thereby broadening its applicability to combinatorial theory. By establishing a relationship between the foundation theorem and the exchange property, we demonstrate that a set of objects sharing the exchange property can be expressed as a union of foundations. Utilizing this connection, we prove the foundation theorem for the involutions within the hyperoctahedral group $H_n$. Observations of Type Ia Supernovae have long served as key distance indicators in cosmology, their utility lying in their relatively stable and explosive behavior.  Despite widespread use, a well-known limitation of these supernovae is their luminosity variation, primarily attributed to progenitor mass differences and welding interactions between the white dwarf and accreted matter.  A less explored effect on their luminosity is the influence of gravitational lensing, specifically magnification due to the bending of light around mass concentrations, be it in the form of clusters, groups, or individual galaxies.  A perfect lensing system would equally distribute the magnification across a circular area around the lens, affecting nearby supernovae to a greater degree than more distant ones.  Since this effect is proportional to the supernova's luminosity rather than absolute magnitude, it would primarily impact their intrinsic brightness rather than their observed redshift.  A simple mathematical model based on the Schnitzler and Weinberg 2007 lensing formula provides an estimate of this impact, with its standard deviation being a significant component of total variation.  Given the relatively small standard deviation compared to other Type Ia dispersion, a reasonable expectation would be that a large sample of supernovae with accurate host galaxy subtraction and minimal foreground contamination could allow the amplification effect to be statistically identified.  Using the Pantheon collection of Type Ia Supernovae and a lensing model adjusted for the specific lensing influence on each supernova, a mild correlation is observed with a statistical significance of over 5 sigma, with a coefficient of determination (R^2) equal to 3.82%, indicating that about 4% of the variation in a plot of absolute magnitude versus redshift could be attributed to the lensing effect.  In a simple linear model, the standard deviation of the amplification distribution is approximately 0.245, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.205 to 0.285, reflecting the influence of gravitational lensing on Type Ia Supernovae.  This discovery opens up a new area of research into the amplification of these supernovae, with potential to offer greater insight into the distribution of mass concentrations across the universe. Our research indicates that neither the neural network nor the word representations used are solely responsible for the observed performance, but rather a complex interaction of all variables. Moreover, a detailed examination of our empirical results reveals insights that could enhance the development of more sophisticated word representations with improved polarity capture properties. Ultimately, our findings suggest that while modern pre-trained models excel in sentiment classification tasks, it is premature to conclude that they comprehensively grasp the complex polarity structure as defined by the Loughran-McDonald dataset. In the context of searching for optimal solutions in multiagent systems, a significant issue arises when agents' actions are influenced by noisy observations. We investigate the performance of an information gathering approach, called Multiagent Rationalizable Equilibria via Search (MARES). MARES is an open-source Python package available on GitHub, incorporating a robust form of the search algorithm introduced in a related publication. We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate MARES's effectiveness in finding rationalizable equilibria at both individual agent and system-wide levels. We also examine the interplay between key parameters and provide a preliminary analysis of the method's applicability in online settings. Moreover, we explore the extraction of informative data through the deployment of MARES in a dynamic environment, revealing an interesting connection between this process and MARES's ability to converge to optimal solutions. A key insight gained from these experiments serves as a foundation for future research in optimizing MARES. An analysis is performed on the effects of interconnecting two separate networks, using the example of two scale-free networks, on the spread of an SIR epidemic in an unknown graph. The degree of the epidemic's impact is measured by the proportion of individuals in the population that remain infected, and this measurement is examined in the context of three scenarios: when the epidemic is limited to one network, and when the epidemic spreads between the two networks with equal probability, as well as in the scenario where the epidemic spreads more easily in the second network. The results show that in all three situations, the shape of the final fraction of infected individuals remains the same over time; however, the speed at which this shape is achieved changes. Furthermore, the opportunity exists to slow the epidemic's spread by selectively rewiring some of the graph's connections in a way that targets specific infected individuals. This approach is found to be effective in reducing the final fraction of infected individuals below what would be expected for a random rewiring strategy. Furthermore, this method is applicable to large populations. The conditions under which the greatest benefit can be obtained from this strategy include rewiring a small number of key connections, and the strategy is successful in reaching a lower fraction of infected individuals than would be obtained from a random rewiring of a smaller number of connections. The results provided in this study are applicable to a broad category of graphs known as complex networks. In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of non-trivial Cotton solitons on these manifolds when they are of type (K). Subsequently, we demonstrate that a non-trivial shrinking Cotton soliton on a (D) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold always corresponds to an umbilical point, while a non-trivial expanding Cotton soliton cannot exist on these manifolds. Moreover, we show that a non-trivial shrinking Cotton soliton on a (C) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold with $\rho(g) \neq 0$ always corresponds to an umbilical point with negative Ricci curvature. If $\rho(g) = 0$, we demonstrate the existence of a non-trivial shrinking Cotton soliton on a (C) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold. The relationship between these findings and the Ricci operator on these manifolds is also explored. Additionally, we establish that a non-trivial expanding Cotton soliton is incompatible with the given curvature conditions on (C) and (D) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Moreover, we demonstrate that if the Ricci operator $\rho$ is an anti-self-adjoint matrix on a (K) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, then it implies the non-existence of a non-trivial shrinking Cotton soliton on these manifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if the Ricci operator $\rho$ is a self-adjoint matrix on a (D) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, then it implies the non-existence of a non-trivial expanding Cotton soliton on these manifolds. The relationship between the curvature conditions and the Schouten tensor on these manifolds is also explored. Additionally, we demonstrate that a non-trivial expanding Cotton soliton on a (C) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold is incompatible with the given curvature conditions. Moreover, we demonstrate that if the Schouten tensor $S$ is an anti-self-adjoint matrix on a (K) Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, then it implies the non-existence of a non-trivial shrinking Cotton soliton on these manifolds

Reinforcement learning is a highly effective method for robot skill learning, however, one major limitation of this approach is the requirement for a vast number of trials to achieve optimal results. A common strategy to circumvent this issue is the use of efficient sampling methods, specifically experience replay. Despite its advantages, the current implementation of this method in RLS is flawed, as it currently fails to account for the varying performance of different episodes. As a result, the optimal policy is often hindered in its pursuit of optimal returns, resulting in poor decision making. To address this shortcoming, a new approach called the variance decrease based experience replay was developed. This approach identifies episodes that contain valuable information for improving the policy and gives them more importance, resulting in a more efficient use of data. The proposed approach is mathematically analyzed and proven to result in a more efficient use of data, and is further demonstrated through successful applications on two challenging robot learning tasks. I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile tool that offers two main features to enhance user productivity when working with quantum operator algebras. Firstly, it provides an intuitive high-level language for defining and managing commutative relationships between various quantum operator bases, making it especially useful for simplifying complex Hamiltonian combinations. Secondly, libcommute offers a detailed diagonalization framework that leverages these defined commutative interactions to transform and simplify the diagonalization of eigenstates, ultimately improving performance by exploiting existing symmetries from a computational perspective. This tool is designed to be useful for both large-scale simulations and in-depth educational exercises concerning quantum operator algebras. A user-friendly interface and extensive documentation are also available to guide users through the process of defining commutative interactions and utilizing the diagonalization framework. A marked version of the code is available at https://github.com/ThomasJaneson/libcommute-lib, while an executable version can be accessed at https://github.com/ThomasJaneson/libcommute-py. The code is based on the commute.py library and builds upon it, with additional features such as nested algebra support, found at https://github.com/ThomasJaneson/commute.py. The libcommute toolkit can be utilized through a command-line interface by running pycommute.sh or pycommute.bat. Full installation instructions are available in the libcommute-pyREADME.md file. The libcommute toolkit was initially developed to support the educational objectives outlined in the companion paper titled "Teaching Matrix Product States and Commutator-Driven Diagonalization" and is now available as an open-source project. The implementation of the toolkit's features, specifically the commute.py library, is reviewed in the technical section of this document, along with a discussion of the technical challenges encountered. Finally, an exploration of the further developments and potential extensions of the libcommute toolkit is presented in the conclusion. The libcommute toolkit has been successfully integrated into the curriculum at the University of Alberta, specifically in the Physics 419 course, as part of a unit focused on quantum teaching. In addition, the toolkit's features have been leveraged to develop the commute game, an interactive educational exercise available at https://github.com/ThomasJaneson/commute-game. The implementation of the toolkit's features has also inspired the creation of the qft tool, an interactive tool designed to guide users through the process of solving first-order quantum field theory problems, available at https://github.com/ThomasJaneson

The crystal structure of the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ superconductor has been reexamined using real-space warrantors, a method previously utilized for the study of graphene and carbon nanotubes, to assess its lattice authenticity. A thorough analysis of the results revealed that previously reported quantities such as critical temperature, magnetic moment, and spin density around the iron atoms could be inaccurately interpreted due to the non-authentic electronic architecture caused by an irregular iron-aspirin configuration. Consequently, a correction was applied to the iron-aspirin arrangement, and a more authentic electronic structure was achieved. Notably, this correction led to a better alignment with experimental findings, specifically regarding the NMR relaxation rate and the superconducting gap size, and it also facilitated a more straightforward interpretation of the magnetic moment and spin density around the iron atoms. Nonetheless, some discrepancies persist, suggesting that slight variations in the iron-aspirin configuration could also be significant in influencing the magnetic behavior of this material. Furthermore, a comparison with a study on (Ba$_{0.88}$K$_{0.82}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ revealed that both a longer superconducting gap and a higher magnetic moment around the iron-aspirin sites correspond with a more asymmetric electron-aspirin configuration. Interestingly, this study discovered that a specific void configuration, consisting of a 25 angstroms sphere centered at the iron-aspirin site, has a significant impact on the magnetic moment around this location. Moreover, a more detailed analysis of the electronic architecture in this material suggests that a topological superconducting state could be induced by increasing the magnetic moment around the iron-aspirin site to a minimum magnitude of 0.3 Bohr magnetons. Furthermore, the results indicate that a more complex iron-aspirin arrangement could facilitate a more stable topological state, and the critical temperature for this state could be enhanced to 5.1 Kelvin. Lastly, our study proposes that a more complex electron-aspirin arrangement might be necessary to achieve high critical temperatures for superconduction in this family of materials. We have conducted an in-depth study of the metallic phase of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR and real-space NMR imaging. Our measurements reveal distinct spin relaxation processes occurring on and off the surface of the samples, allowing us to gather spatially resolved magnetic relaxation data. The obtained data demonstrate that the surface and bulk components of the samples exhibit different spin relaxation times, with the surface showing faster relaxation. This distinction becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures, with a corresponding decrease in the spin density as indicated by the NMR signal intensity. Notably, the proportion of surface to bulk contributions can be adjusted through the thickness of the LaNiO$_3$ layer, with implications for our understanding of the surface and interface effects in these superlattices. Furthermore, our study observes a broader NMR line width in thicker samples, attributing this to enhanced spin density and the resulting magnetic interaction at the interface. Our research contributes valuable insights to the broader study of these superlattices, enabling further exploration of their electronic structure and the influence of spin-orbit coupling. Ultimately, our $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR and real-space NMR imaging results provide a foundation for the interpretation of existing and future data in this research area.

Furthermore, the robot's ability to recover energy from its actuator during single step tests demonstrates its potential for efficient and resilient bipedal movement. To take advantage of this feature, a simple control system is proposed that utilizes sensory feedback to match the actuator's resonance frequency with the robot's movement period. Successful application of this control system resulted in a 75% decrease in average power and a 50% reduction in peak power during multiple step tests. However, the system needs further improvement to handle the impacts associated with larger steps. To address this issue, a possible design modification and an alternative control strategy are also presented in this study. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

In this study, we examine how this newer data impact the minimum masses achievable for neutrino flavors other than electron anti-neutrinos. Utilizing a simplified model where neutrino flavors possess equal masses and form a continuous spectrum upon oscillating, we determined the best and worst-case scenarios for constraining these masses through electron anti-neutrino research. The newer KATRIN findings reduce the best-case constraint on these masses by a factor of two to sixteen, with the worst-case scenario seeing a constraint increase to 1.3 times the existing standard. The general case, where neutrino flavors do not oscillate, sees the best-case constraint improved to 0.6 eV/c^2 and the worst-case scenario rise to 1.5 times the current standard. The fundamental question remains of whether future research projects such as KATRIN or its upgrades could potentially discover minimum neutrino masses below the present threshold of 0.1 eV/c^2. In the context of the simpler model used here, we establish that achieving this goal would require further restrictions on the standard three-flavor neutrino paradigm, likely involving constraints on neutrino flavor mixing parameters of no more than on the order of 10^-5 for the best-case scenario, or alternatively, placing limits on the sum of all neutrino masses at a level no higher than on the order of 0.5 eV/c^2 for the worst-case scenario. The former requirement presents a challenge to implementing the necessary protocols to meet the desired outcome, but the latter presents a feasible path towards achieving this goal. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from two-dimensional images is a difficult face processing task due to frequent occlusions caused by hats, sunglasses, and other obstructions. This challenging issue is compounded by the significant variation in face appearances caused by different poses, ages, and expression levels. As a result, many parts of a face are often difficult to model accurately using existing methods, which usually focus on fitting entire face shapes at once. This paper introduces a novel approach called SADRNet, which breaks down the face into two distinct components - one for the occluded left half and one for the visible right half. This allows for separate regression networks to be trained on a vast collection of face images, resulting in significant improvement in density-based face alignment and three-dimensional face reconstruction compared to existing methods. Experimental results show that SADRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple face alignment benchmarks, including a self-evaluation test on a dataset containing a wide range of face images that are heavily occluded or only partially visible. This method's ability to accurately model hidden face parts is a major breakthrough in three-dimensional face reconstruction from two-dimensional images. It can be applied to various real-world scenarios such as virtual avatars, video surveillance, and border control, among others. Due to its complex design involving multiple regression networks and a self-alignment process, it may be difficult to apply SADRNet in simple face-based systems without extensive face knowledge. As a result, a simplified version of this approach called SRNet is also presented for consideration in such systems. SRNet's performance, however, falls short of SADRNet's performance on all benchmark tests. In order to apply SADRNet in various face-based systems, a detailed guide, including a sample implementation, is also provided for easy integration into any face processing code. Furthermore, both SADRNet and SRNet are an open-source solutions that are available for download from https://github.com/taehwan-kim/SADRNet. In addition to providing a novel solution to the face reconstruction challenge, this work also introduces an innovative way to model hidden face components, such as occlusions caused by hats and sunglasses. This investigation seeks to examine the techniques being proposed to enhance the accuracy of manual ballot count efforts, with a particular focus on the method known as Informed OCR (iOCR). This method aims to enhance the performance of optical character recognition (OCR) technology by integrating context-related information when matching characters. To evaluate iOCR, a set of tests was conducted using a dataset compiled from actual election results, with the goal of comparing its effectiveness against both traditional OCR methods and machine learning-based approaches. The results indicate that iOCR yields superior outcomes, with an overall accuracy rate of 42% in correcting errors from an initial OCR process, representing a notable improvement over the 29% achieved by machine learning-based methods and the 21% achieved by conventional OCR techniques. Furthermore, it was found that one of the primary sources of errors in the data set is the inconsistent use of commas as thousand separators, with a simple pre-processing step able to address this issue by standardizing this practice. Following pre-processing, the accuracy of the system as a whole increases to 57%. The study also highlights the potential benefits of adapting machine learning models to tolerate minor discrepancies in formatting, with such modifications resulting in a further enhancement of accuracy to 63%. The research concludes by exploring the possibilities of combining the proposed method with other data validation techniques to achieve even greater gains in accuracy. With the aim of facilitating the development of advanced formats for ballot counts that can be accurately scanned using OCR technology, the study also highlights the challenges associated with configuring machine learning models to format-specific data sets. The opportunity for collaborative research on these topics is also presented. The investigation further highlights the need to develop more sophisticated methods for evaluating the performance of OCR systems on real-world data sets, with a particular emphasis on the inclusion of semantic validation techniques. The study also showcases the utility of the test suite it developed, with a likelihood of it being relevant to a broader range of manual data entry tasks. The research concludes by highlighting the potential of iOCR to be integrated with other data validation techniques, as well as its potential for collaboration and further investigation into more advanced methods. Noisy speech enhancement is a complex issue with numerous potential applications, including better audio for people who are hard of hearing and improved speech recognition performance. This paper proposes a comprehensive attention bidirectional deep learning framework that leverages complex neural networks to effectively mitigate background noise. This proposed framework involves two key components. Firstly, a complex multi-dimensional attention mechanism is used to pinpoint the optimal spectral bins for each frequency sub-band by comparing the noisy speech spectrum with a set of learned clean speech spectra. Secondly, a complex bidirectional long short-term memory layer is employed to craft a more accurate representation of the time-domain audio by modeling the relationships between clean speech features at adjacent time frames. Experimental results show that this proposed framework yields superior performance to existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of signal-to-noise ratio improvement and subjective quality. Furthermore, this framework's ability to improve speech recognition accuracy has been successfully demonstrated. Our FDTree approach provides a versatile framework for evaluating the quality of RDF datasets, and we anticipate it to contribute positively to this research area. This study presents new findings from the analysis of a large sample of 80 Seyfert galaxies, focusing on their ionized gas patterns. Despite initial predictions, we did not find significant evidence supporting a standard "biconical" shape associated with active galactic nuclei. Instead, we detected a more common alternative where the ionization axis lies at an angle greater than 45 degrees to our line of sight. This occurrence is particularly prevalent among low-luminosity Seyfert galaxies. In a surprising breakthrough, our analysis revealed a distinct relationship between gas ionization angles and host galaxy properties, specifically velocity. This connection was most pronounced in the outer regions of the gas clouds. In contrast, gas inside the inner regions revealed a more complex velocity pattern, linked to multiple sources, including a rotating gas disk, a retrograde disk, and a prograde disk. Notably, we discovered a critical angle of 45 degrees, below which the velocity pattern becomes irregular. This irregularity may be caused by gas ionized by shock waves. We also established a limit on shock densities and suggested a possible explanation for the narrow emission lines observed in Mrk 79. Our study introduces a new method to distinguish between shock and AGN ionization and paves the way for further investigation into the interplay between gas dynamics, host galaxy properties, and the influence of active galactic nuclei. This discovery may imply a role for galaxy interactions in shaping the ionized gas patterns and velocity structures. As a result, we propose a new scenario where a combination of a small-scale black hole and a large-scale nuclear bar could be responsible for the detected patterns. This finding highlights the importance of considering multiple ionization processes and gas dynamics in the interpretation of spectral data. It also emphasizes the need for a broader perspective that takes into account the host galaxy's interactions and scale, rather than a narrow focus on active galactic nuclei. This study demonstrates the value of collecting and analyzing a large dataset of 100 Seyfert galaxies, obtained from the Odyssé and OSIRIS spectrograph databases, made available by the University of Sydney and Leiden University. These findings provide a solid foundation for further research into the complex processes occurring in active galactic nuclei and the host galaxy's environment. The development of advanced driving algorithms requires vast amounts of high-quality data, enabling them to learn from numerous examples and adapt to diverse situations. Current methods for generating realistic traffic scenes through random sampling or style transfer have several limitations: they often produce repetitive scenes, differ significantly from actual scenes, and cannot accurately account for the relationships between objects in the scene. To address these challenges, we propose SceneGen, a novel approach that utilizes a unique combination of techniques. SceneGen represents a scene as a sequence of interconnected events, with each event defined by the participating objects' positions, their interactive relationships (such as collisions, connections, and isolated actions), and their spatial boundaries. By drawing from real-world datasets, we train a series of models that can accurately model the distribution of objects' positions, their interactive relationships, and the scene's spatial organization. These models work together to generate a diverse range of authentic scenes that accurately capture the statistical characteristics of actual scenes. Our results demonstrate SceneGen's superiority over existing methods, producing a more substantial variety of high-quality scenes that are visually indistinguishable from real traffic scenes. These scenes are equally effective when used in training and testing autonomous driving algorithms. Notably, our approach enables us to generate an infinite number of unique scenes using a fixed set of objects, unlike other methods that rely on random sampling or transform-based techniques and struggle to produce more than 10,000 unique scenes. We open-source SceneGen to contribute to the development of more advanced driving algorithms and to encourage other researchers to explore similar approaches in adjacent fields. We also release a comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses the realism of generated scenes and their effectiveness in improving the performance of autonomous driving algorithms. This framework includes a real-world dataset containing over 50,000 high-quality, annotated traffic scenes, available for download from https://traffic.scenegen.io/. We demonstrate SceneGen's potential to produce high-quality scenes in multiple cities by adapting its models to traffic environments in Beijing, Berlin, and San Francisco. Our results show that SceneGen's models generalize exceptionally well, producing a mere 2% of scenes that are city-specific, even after being trained on data from multiple cities. We believe SceneGen's unique event-driven approach marks a significant breakthrough in generating realistic traffic scenes. It overcomes several limitations of current methods and yields a more substantial variety of authentic scenes that accurately capture the statistical characteristics of actual scenes. These high-quality scenes are equally effective when used in training and testing autonomous driving algorithms. We open-source SceneGen to contribute to the development of more advanced driving algorithms

Researchers seek to establish conditions under which multiple coexisting phases emerge in statistical mechanics models, such as the Ising model, by creating periodic configurations through weak periodic extensions. In this study, we introduce a novel, weaker concept of periodicity applicable to Gibbs measures and utilize it to develop a technique for evaluating the stability of these measures. By employing this method, we demonstrate our findings by analyzing the Cayley tree graph and the complete graph. On the Cayley tree graph, we are able to identify a precise condition for multiple coexisting phases in the Ising model and demonstrate its efficacy through numerical simulations. In contrast, the Ising model exhibits a non-trivial phase transition on the complete graph. Interestingly, restricting the Ising model to finite parameters also results in a non-trivial phase transition on the complete graph, despite the fact that in infinite dimensions, the model's behavior is closely related to that of the model on the Cayley tree. Notably, we discovered a new, sharp stability condition for the Ising model on the Cayley tree through our analysis, and it significantly surpasses previously known conditions for weak periodicity. The newly developed technique for evaluating the stability of periodic configurations also enables us to identify a new, sharp condition for the Ising model's phase coexistence on the complete graph. The results presented in this study provide a theoretical foundation for further investigation of the Ising model's properties and are accessible through a web interface designed for this purpose. The interface allows users to customize parameters such as the degree of the graph, the number of components in the graph, the Ising model's parameters, and the periodic configuration, and it enables the determination of a specific, sharp stability condition for the Ising model on the Cayley tree and the complete graph. The web interface can be found at the following link: http://m3.runit.csail.mit.edu:8080/periodicity/. The web interface can also be accessed through the MIT CSAIL homepage. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is a crucial capability for self-driving cars, given the need to allow them to safely navigate roads even when they're far away. Current 3D object detection algorithms often fall short in this regard because they can be compromised by limited pixel data available at long ranges. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel 3D detection framework called Far3Det, designed to identify distant objects by leveraging 2D detections in a semi-supervised manner. By doing so, we're able to harness the vast quantity of annotated 2D data to inform our 3D distance estimation. To further improve performance, we've also developed a new score function that penalizes inconsistencies between 2D and 3D measurements, allowing us to refine our estimates through iterative optimization. To support our claims, we've conducted thorough evaluations on the Argoverse dataset, demonstrating superior distance estimation accuracy and overall 3D MAP performance compared to existing approaches. Notably, Far3Det has achieved notable success in detecting distant objects, with a significant improvement in the AP metric at far ranges. To complement these findings, we've also analyzed the performance of our method on a subset of challenging scenarios and have made our code publicly available for ease of replication. Despite the progress made, we've identified several areas for further research to fully address the complex issues in this domain. Lastly, we've established a new benchmark called Far3Det-Benchmark, consisting of a range-based annotation interface that could serve as a reference framework for other distance estimation benchmarks. With this benchmark in place, we hope to spark more innovations in this area and provide a starting point for developers to explore the possibilities of Far3Det. In the evaluation section of our paper, we've provided a detailed breakdown of our results, including a distance distribution analysis and an examination of the performance of our method on a subset of challenging scenarios. These results demonstrate the superiority of Far3Det over existing 3D detection baselines and confirm our design choices. Furthermore, we've explored potential ways to integrate Far3Det with external information sources, such as map data, to further enhance its performance. Overall, our research has made substantial contributions to the advancement of 3D object detection at great distances, with a focus on the design of distance-aware loss functions and semi-supervised learning from 2D detections. By combining these components, we've developed a highly optimized Far3Det framework that outperforms all existing 3D detection baselines on the Argoverse validation set

For autonomous navigation, scene flow estimation is a crucial capability to model a vehicle's movement and surrounding environment. However, this task is complicated by the large amount of visual data required and the need to accurately account for a vehicle's field of view which typically covers about 45 degrees in all directions. Many approaches fail to account for the impact of a vehicle's surrounding environment on its neighbors and often don't consider how to effectively apply previously learned knowledge to this task. In our research, we address these limitations by introducing a novel metric-based training method that utilizes unlabelled bridge images to enhance a scene flow estimation model's performance on ramp images. This method involves initially pre-training the model to recognize features on bridge images and then utilizing its ability to recognize features on ramp images. The model's performance is optimized based on the flow metric and a self-correcting technique that reduces the impact of noisy labels from unlabelled ramp images. Our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and produces more reliable results than competitive approaches that we tested. Our code is available online at https://github.com/zheng-hao-adaptive/MTSFE.

Recently, introducing randomness into neural networks has been proven beneficial in hastening the convergence speed of neural networks through mutual neural network training. However, the method's potential for categorization after training has not been thoroughly explored. In this paper, we test the hypothesis that a random neural network can be used for efficient and accurate data categorization by fine-tuning its weights after training. To achieve this, we utilize a spiking random neural network with unique learning rules that differentiate between training and categorization phases. The model's performance is demonstrated on various datasets, revealing improved accuracy and a significant reduction in computational resources when compared to traditional neural networks. For instance, the model exhibits exceptional performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a minimal error rate of 8.57%, outperforming all comparable recent studies. In addition, the model's capacity to achieve precise categorization with reduced precision was also found to result in a substantial decrease in energy consumption during training, representing a potential area for further optimization. In terms of energy efficiency during categorization, the model reveals potential for improvement, with an average energy consumption of 37.14% less than the base line, indicating an avenue for enhanced fine-tuning. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering rules in containers, enabling the isolation of microservices. High-resolution subsurface reconstruction through seismic imaging has the potential to be achieved via expanded source waveform inversion, a newly proposed method that maps observed data to Earth's properties by solving for an expanded source model and wavefield mapping the Earth's interior. However, solving this highly nonlinear problem requires a significant number of computational resources, especially given that traditional time-domain wavefield simulations are inherently costly. As an alternative, a wavefield approximation is suggested, derived from the adjoint state computational approach, which inherently accounts for earth property variations and source morphology. By leveraging this approximation, the expensive computation of wavefield simulations can be replaced with a significantly more affordable forward modeling system, consisting of a short-range scattering operator that simulates time-domain wavefields on the basis of an expanded source model and structural parameters. In this work in progress, we discuss the theoretical basis for this approximation and its resulting simplified modeling system. We also present some preliminary numerical results demonstrating its computational efficiency and potential in delivering high-resolution earth property images without the need for complex wavefield transformations. Despite these promising findings, further investigation is required to fully evaluate the method's performance and potential limitations. In particular, we require further analysis of how the approximation behaves under diverse seismic data configurations and scattering operator properties. Additionally, we aim to conduct a comparative assessment of this method's efficiency, accuracy, and sensitivity in relation to traditional waveform inversion. Furthermore, we intend to explore the expanded source waveform inversion's applicability to real-world field data sets. In the context of this study, we propose a simplified expanded source waveform inversion framework that utilizes an approximate wavefield model, derived from the adjoint state computational approach, as a computational model. This framework's performance will be evaluated based on comparative computational cost, earth property resolution, and accuracy in relation to traditional time-domain waveform inversion. Some preliminary results indicate that this method yields comparable earth property images to those obtained via time-domain waveform inversion at a significantly lower computational cost per iteration. Nevertheless, further investigation is needed to fully assess this method's performance, potential, and limitations. In the long term, this study's findings have the potential to guide the development of advanced seismic imaging techniques that deliver high-resolution earth property images at a lower computational cost. In the context of deep learning-based seismic imaging methods, the insights gained from this investigation can be used to design more efficient neural network architectures that deliver high-resolution earth property images quickly. As such, this study's outcomes will be significant in the seismic imaging domain, with potential applications across various fields such as geology, engineering, and environmental science

We've demonstrated the integration of two distinct phenomena - quantum compression and optical asymmetry - in a combined scheme involving a quantum mirror and an asymmetric cavity.  While both phenomena exhibit remarkable potential, their inherent limitations hinder their utility in certain applications.  For instance, the difficulty in achieving high-Q factors in dielectric materials restricts the efficacy of optical asymmetry.  On the other hand, quantum compression offers a means to reduce the size of optical components, but its implementation is complicated by the need to maintain low loss levels in thin sections of dielectric materials.  However, when these two phenomena are integrated, we observe significant compression factors (up to 25) along with low loss tangents (below 10^-3) in our integrated optical components.  Furthermore, our design allows for a wide range of parameter combinations that can be optimized for various applications through simple numerical extraction of the S parameters of the quantum mirror element.  We validate our approach through both theoretical modeling and experimental verification.  We construct an example of an integrated optical voltage sensor based on this concept, where a polymer mirror is integrated into an air-spaced etalon to detect alcohol, with a minimum detectable pressure of 5.6 kPa and a sensitivity of 0.024 nm/kPa.  This integrated approach has the potential to simplify the design of complex optical systems while providing greater flexibility in component selection.  While our demonstration focuses on an asymmetric etalon, the same principles can be applied to other complex optical components with added benefits of high reflectivity and transmissivity at the mirror interfaces, allowing for even greater compression factors than achieved here.  Nonetheless, this approach is particularly well-suited for applications involving low loss tangents and minimal optical asymmetry, such as deflection, modulation, and non-linear interactions.  We foresee this integrated approach enabling the development of compact, low loss optical systems that can handle high power levels.  Furthermore, our design allows for the integration of multiple quantum mirrors, enabling the creation of complex optical systems from a variety of combined components, enabling new functions that were previously unattainable with traditional bulk components. The current trend in conversational evaluation focuses solely on the generated text, neglecting the underlying conversation history. This gap in understanding led us to investigate whether the encoder representations used in these models contain sufficient information about the turn assignment. Our findings show that these representations are inadequate, as demonstrated by the substantial performance gain achieved by a simple baseline model that predicts the turn based on the generated text alone. This prediction accuracy surpasses that of a state-of-the-art turn-aware conversation model. Building upon this discovery, we introduced a more rigorous evaluation framework that considers both the turn assignment and the quality of generated text. Our framework comprises three primary components: (1) a turn-aware metric that assesses a model's turn prediction capabilities and rewards high-quality text generation, (3) a turn-agnostic metric that evaluates the produced text in isolation, and (4) a diverse data set of turn-annotated conversations for each benchmark dataset. Our results indicate that optimizing models for these metrics yields superior performance on both turn prediction and text quality, as well as enhanced generalizability. We incorporated this framework into a publicly available repository that provides actionable insights for model selection and showcases the advantages of a simple baseline model. We also introduce an interactive tool that enables users to explore the turn assignment representations used in pre-trained conversation models. This repository is available at https://github.com/aleksamelnik/turn-eval. We hope that by incorporating a turn-aware perspective into the evaluation of conversation models, we can pave the way for the development of more sophisticated, turn-informed language generation algorithms.
